etymology: Hebrew Bezeq, perhaps “lightning” or “sowing”; a place in the land of Canaan given into Judah’s hand, and, it seems, a mustering-ground in Israel.
biblical_def: When Judah went up to take her inheritance, “the LORD delivered the Canaanites and the Perizzites into their hand” at Bezek, and there they slew ten thousand men (Jdg 1:4). The victory was not Judah’s sword but the LORD’s gift; the tribe went up at His word, and He gave the enemy into her hand. At Bezek they found Adoni-bezek, the lord of the place, and when they had taken him and cut off his thumbs and his great toes, he confessed the righteousness of his own doom: threescore and ten kings, he said, had gathered their meat under his table with thumbs and toes cut off, and as he had done, so God had requited him. The cruel man was measured by his own measure, and the mouth of the tyrant justified the judgment of God. Bezek is therefore a witness that the LORD reigns over the nations and repays the proud oppressor in his own coin. Long after, the same name saw Saul number Israel — three hundred thousand of Israel and thirty thousand of Judah (1Sa 11:8) — and march to deliver Jabesh-gilead. The ground that saw the Canaanite broken saw Israel gathered as one man to save her brethren. Learn here that vengeance belongs to the LORD, that He humbles the cruel, and that He raises up deliverance for His people even where the wicked fell.
webster_summary: A place in Canaan where the LORD delivered the Canaanites into Judah’s hand and Adoni-bezek confessed God’s just recompense (Jdg 1:4); later Saul’s muster to save Jabesh-gilead (1Sa 11:8).

etymology: Hebrew Qarqor, perhaps “level ground” or “foundation”; a place in the eastern wilderness beyond Jordan where the kings of Midian encamped.
biblical_def: Beyond Jordan, when Gideon had chased the kings of Midian across the wilderness, “Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor, and their hosts with them, about fifteen thousand men, all that were left of all the hosts of the children of the east” (Jdg 8:10). A hundred and twenty thousand that drew sword had already fallen, and the fifteen thousand that remained thought themselves safe, far from the battle, at their ease in Karkor. But no distance shelters the enemy of God, and no host is secure that has lifted itself against His people. Gideon fell upon them while the host was secure, and put all the host to flight, and took the two kings. The three hundred who began with lamps and pitchers finished the rout at Karkor, that all Israel might see the salvation was of the LORD and not of numbers. Here is the comfort of the church against her proud adversaries: they may be many and confident, encamped in their supposed safety, but the LORD needs neither multitude nor might to scatter them. The Midianite that oppressed Israel seven years was broken by a faint and weary band, that no flesh should glory. Karkor preaches that the confident foe is never beyond the reach of the arm of the LORD, and that the weakness of His servants is the very theatre of His strength.

etymology: Hebrew Qamon, perhaps “standing-place” or “full of stalks”; a town of Gilead beyond Jordan, the burial-place of Jair the judge.
biblical_def: After Gideon and Abimelech, Jair the Gileadite judged Israel two and twenty years, and had thirty sons that rode on thirty ass colts; and when his course was finished the record is brief and solemn: “And Jair died, and was buried in Camon” (Jdg 10:5). One line closes a life of rule. Camon is the grave of a judge, and it preaches the appointed end of every servant of God, however long his labour or many his honours. The judges were raised up in their generations to deliver Israel, and each in his turn laid down his office and his life and went the way of all the earth. Yet the burial of the LORD’s servant is not the defeat of the LORD’s work; the God who raised up Jair raised up Jephthah after him, and the succession of deliverers failed not until the great Deliverer came. The people of God are mortal, but the purpose of God is not. Camon reminds the church that her ministers and her judges are earthen vessels, given for a season and then gathered to their fathers, while the treasure abides and the Lord of the harvest is never without a labourer. Blessed are the dead which die in the LORD, for they rest from their labours; and the servant buried in Camon awaits, with all the redeemed, the multitude that no man can number before the throne.
webster_summary: A town in Gilead where Jair the Gileadite judge was buried (Jdg 10:5); a witness to the appointed end of the LORD’s servants.

etymology: Hebrew Chermon, “devoted” or “sacred mountain,” from a root to devote or set apart; the great snow-capped mountain on the northern border of the land.
biblical_def: Hermon lifts its snow-crowned head at the northern border of the promised land, the great mountain from whose feet the springs of Jordan flow. When Israel took the land east of Jordan, they took it “from the river of Arnon unto mount Hermon” (Deu 3:8), and Joshua smote the kings even unto Baalgad in the valley of Lebanon under mount Hermon (Jos 11:17); the mountain stood as the appointed bound of the inheritance the LORD had measured for His people. But Hermon is best known for its dew. The psalmist likens the blessing of brotherly love to “the dew of Hermon, and as the dew that descended upon the mountains of Zion: for there the LORD commanded the blessing, even life for evermore” (Psa 133:3). As the heavy night-dew of that high mountain falls silent and abundant, watering the ground while men sleep, so the LORD pours His blessing where His people dwell together in unity. The blessing is commanded — it is not earned by the brethren but ordained by the LORD, who joins the descent of the dew to the descent of grace. Hermon therefore preaches two truths at once: that the LORD sets the very bounds of His people’s habitation, and that within those bounds He commands the dew of His Spirit upon the communion of the saints, even life for evermore.
webster_summary: The great snow-crowned mountain at the northern bound of the land, whose dew figures the commanded blessing of brotherly unity (Deu 3:8; Psa 133:3).

etymology: Hebrew Lebanon, “the white,” from laban, white, for its snows and pale limestone; the cedar-clad range on the north of the land.
biblical_def: Lebanon is the range of cedars that walls the land upon the north, and Scripture makes it a figure of strength, glory, and fruitfulness. Moses longed to cross Jordan and behold “that goodly mountain, and Lebanon” (Deu 3:25), the good land he might see but not enter. Its chief treasure was its timber: when Solomon would build the house of the LORD, he sent to Hiram, “command thou that they hew me cedar trees out of Lebanon” (1Ki 5:6), for none could skill to hew timber like the Sidonians, and the cedars of Lebanon were carried down to raise the temple at Jerusalem. Thus the glory of Lebanon was given to the house of God — the strongest and most fragrant wood of the earth spent upon the sanctuary where the LORD set His name. The prophet promised that same glory to the redeemed wilderness: “the glory of Lebanon shall be given unto it” (Isa 35:2). And the psalmist takes the cedar as the emblem of the righteous man: “he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon” (Psa 92:12), deep-rooted, evergreen, enduring, planted in the courts of the LORD. Lebanon preaches that the noblest things of creation are given for the worship of God, and that the man who is planted in His house shall flourish tall and unfading, a living cedar in the temple not made with hands.
webster_summary: The cedar-clothed northern range whose timber built the temple, and whose cedar figures the flourishing of the righteous (Deu 3:25; 1Ki 5:6; Psa 92:12).

etymology: Hebrew Sharon, “a plain” or “level place”; the fertile coastal lowland running from Joppa toward Carmel.
biblical_def: Sharon is the broad and fertile plain that runs along the sea from Joppa toward Carmel, a byword in Israel for pasture and flower. There David set his herds, “over the herds that fed in Sharon was Shitrai the Sharonite” (1Ch 27:29), for its rich meadows fed the king’s cattle. When Isaiah would paint the glory of the redeemed creation, he joined it to Sharon: the desert shall blossom, and “the excellency of Carmel and Sharon, they shall see the glory of the LORD” (Isa 35:2). The wilderness that sin made barren the LORD clothes again with the fruitfulness of Sharon, that His people may behold His glory in the flowering of the waste. Above all, Sharon is glorified in the Song, where the Beloved says, “I am the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valleys” (Son 2:1). The church has ever read that rose as her Lord, the fairest among ten thousand, springing up in beauty amid the plain of this world, fragrant and lovely to His people. What Sharon is among the fields — excellent, fruitful, adorned — Christ is among the sons of men, and more. Sharon therefore preaches the beauty the LORD restores to a cursed earth, and points beyond every earthly bloom to the Rose of Sharon Himself, in whom the desolate soul finds fragrance, fruitfulness, and the glory of God.
webster_summary: The fertile coastal plain, byword of pasture and bloom, whose Rose the church reads as her Lord (Isa 35:2; Son 2:1; 1Ch 27:29).

etymology: Hebrew Goshen, of uncertain meaning, perhaps “drawing near”; the fertile region of the eastern Egyptian Delta where Jacob’s house dwelt.
biblical_def: Goshen was the best of the land of Egypt, the pasture in the north-east where Joseph settled his father and his brethren: “thou shalt dwell in the land of Goshen…thou, and thy children, and thy children’s children” (Gen 45:10). Pharaoh himself bade Joseph make his kindred dwell in the best of the land (Gen 47:6), and there the seventy souls of Jacob’s house grew into a great nation. Goshen is first a monument of providence: the God who sent Joseph before them into Egypt prepared a fat and sheltered land to nourish the covenant seed until the appointed hour of the Exodus. But Goshen shines brightest under the plagues. When the LORD smote Egypt, He said, “I will sever in that day the land of Goshen, in which my people dwell, that no swarms of flies shall be there” (Exo 8:22). While judgment fell thick on the Egyptian, Goshen stood untouched, that Pharaoh might know the LORD is in the midst of the earth and makes a difference between His people and the world. Here is the doctrine of discriminating grace set forth in a map: the same land, the same plagues, and yet a people sealed and spared. God still sets His Goshen in the midst of a perishing world, and His covenant to Abraham — “in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed” (Gen 12:3) — is kept safe in the sheltered dwelling of His own.

etymology: Hebrew Elath or Eloth, “grove of great trees,” from elah, a terebinth or mighty tree; a port at the head of the eastern arm of the Red Sea.
biblical_def: Elath, or Eloth, stood at the head of the eastern arm of the Red Sea, hard by Ezion-geber, the last landmark of Israel’s wilderness march by Edom: they passed by from their brethren the children of Esau, dwelling in Seir, “through the way of the plain from Elath” (Deu 2:8). In the days of the kingdom it became a gate to the sea. There Solomon made his navy: “king Solomon made a navy of ships in Eziongeber, which is beside Eloth, on the shore of the Red sea, in the land of Edom” (1Ki 9:26), and from that port his fleet sailed to Ophir and brought home gold, that the wealth of far countries might serve the throne of David’s son. Long after, when the harbour had been lost, Uzziah “built Elath, and restored it to Judah” (2Ki 14:22), and the reach of the kingdom stretched again to the sea. Elath preaches the dominion the LORD grants His anointed king, whose border runs to the uttermost port and whose ships gather the riches of the nations. In Solomon’s navy the church sees a shadow of the greater Son of David, of whom it is written that “the kings of Tarshish and of the isles shall bring presents” (Psa 72:10). The little Red Sea harbour points to a kingdom whose bounds are the ends of the earth, and to a King whom the wealth of the Gentiles shall serve.
webster_summary: The Red Sea port by Ezion-geber, gate of Solomon’s navy, recovered by Uzziah (Deu 2:8; 1Ki 9:26; 2Ki 14:22).

In Solomon’s navy sailing from Elath the church beholds a shadow of the greater Son of David, of whom it is written that the kings of Tarshish and of the isles shall bring presents, and whose kingdom is bounded only by the ends of the earth.

etymology: Hebrew Karmel, “fruitful field” or “garden-land”; here a town in the hill-country of Judah, not the mountain of the same name.
biblical_def: This Carmel is not the great headland where Elijah met the prophets of Baal, but a town in the hill-country of Judah, numbered with Maon and Ziph and Juttah (Jos 15:55), the home of Nabal the churl and Abigail his wife. There “was a man in Maon, whose possessions were in Carmel…he had three thousand sheep, and a thousand goats: and he was shearing his sheep in Carmel” (1Sa 25:2). It was at this sheepshearing, a feast of plenty, that Nabal railed on David’s young men and returned churlish evil for the shelter David’s band had given his flocks. Carmel of Judah is therefore the stage of a great lesson in providence and grace. Nabal is wealth without wisdom, a great man whose name means fool, whose heart was merry with wine while judgment stood at his door; and within ten days the LORD smote him, that he died. Abigail is the prudent wife whose humble speech turned away David from the blood he was hastening to shed, and saved him from avenging himself with his own hand. Here the LORD teaches His anointed to stay his sword and leave vengeance to God, who repaid Nabal without David’s help; for “righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people” (Pro 14:34). Carmel of Judah preaches the folly of riches without grace, and the wisdom that restrains the hand and trusts the LORD to judge.
webster_summary: A town in the hill-country of Judah, home of Nabal and Abigail, where David’s vengeance was restrained (Jos 15:55; 1Sa 25:2); not Mount Carmel.
webster_full: CARMEL (of Judah), a town in the hill-country of Judah.
Numbered with Maon, Ziph, and Juttah (Jos 15:55).
There Nabal sheared his three thousand sheep (1Sa 25:2).
Abigail’s wisdom turned David from avenging himself.
Not the mountain of Elijah, but a town of the south.

corruption_summary: The town of Nabal’s folly and Abigail’s wisdom; it recovers the emptiness of wealth without grace and the restraint of private vengeance.
corruption_paragraphs: This Carmel is a town of Judah, and it keeps no quarrel with the present age; its memory is the sheepshearing of Nabal and the wise intercession of Abigail. It must be distinguished from Mount Carmel, the great headland where Elijah met the prophets of Baal.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that riches without grace are folly, and that vengeance belongs to the LORD. Nabal was a great man and a churl, whose name means fool, and within ten days the LORD smote him; David was stayed by Abigail’s prudence from washing his own hands in blood, and learned to leave his cause with God, who repaid the fool without the sword of the king.

etymology: Hebrew Nephtoach, “an opening,” from pathach, to open, of an opened spring; a fountain on the border of Judah and Benjamin.
biblical_def: Nephtoah was a spring on the hill-country border between Judah and Benjamin, named in the survey of the inheritance where the line ran “unto the fountain of the water of Nephtoah” (Jos 15:9) and again in Benjamin’s lot, “to the well of waters of Nephtoah” (Jos 18:15). It is a small thing, a wayside spring, and yet the Holy Ghost took care to write it into the record, for it marked where one tribe’s portion ended and another’s began. The land was not seized by the strong and grasped by the greedy; it was measured out by lot at the commandment of the LORD, tribe by tribe, boundary by boundary, down to the last fountain and landmark. Nephtoah preaches the exactness of divine providence in the dividing of the inheritance. The God who “hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation” (Act 17:26) appoints not the great borders only but the little springs between them, that every family in Israel might know its own and rest content in the portion He assigned. So the saints have an inheritance measured and kept for them, of which the Lord Himself is the portion, who says to His anointed, “Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance” (Psa 2:8). The boundary-spring of Nephtoah teaches the soul to bless the hand that draws its lot and to say, the lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places.
webster_summary: A boundary-spring between Judah and Benjamin, marking each tribe’s portion (Jos 15:9; Jos 18:15).
webster_full: NEPHTOAH, a spring on the border of Judah and Benjamin.
The line of Judah ran to the fountain of Nephtoah (Jos 15:9).
The lot of Benjamin reached the well of Nephtoah (Jos 18:15).
A small spring, yet a landmark of the inheritance.
A witness to the exactness of God in dividing the land.

corruption_summary: The boundary-spring of the two tribes; it recovers the exactness of divine providence in apportioning the inheritance.
corruption_paragraphs: Nephtoah is a wayside spring on an old tribal border, and it keeps no quarrel with the present age; its quiet lesson is the care of God in the smallest landmark of the inheritance.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the exactness of divine providence. The land was not seized by the strong but measured out by lot at the LORD’s commandment, tribe by tribe, down to the last fountain; and the God who determined the bounds of their habitation appoints not the great borders only but the little springs between them, that every family might rest content in the portion He assigned. So the saints have an inheritance measured and kept, of which the LORD Himself is the portion.
